subject: Banking
title: Why Rogue Traders Keep Happening
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Why Rogue Traders Keep Happening.

hook.text: Every decade produces new rogue traders. Despite billions spent on compliance.

buildup.text: The pattern repeats: a trader hides small losses, doubles down, and the losses compound until discovery.

discovery.text: Banks incentivize risk-taking with huge bonuses tied to profits.

twist.text: Rogue traders are always caught after the losses grow massive.

climax.text: Rogue trading isn't a bug in banking — it's a feature of the incentive structure.

punchline.text: Star performer or rogue trader. The only difference is whether the bet won.

quiz.question: Why do rogue trader incidents keep recurring?
options: Banking incentives reward risk-taking while treating oversight as a cost center

details.summary: Rogue trading scandals repeat across decades because banks incentivize massive risk-taking with bonuses, maintain inadequate controls, and often ignore warning signs when a trader appears to be generating large profits.
details.whyItMatters: The pattern of rogue trading reveals structural problems in banking culture. Until incentives change and risk controls are genuinely independent, unauthorized trading will continue to cause billion-dollar losses.
takeaways: Bonus structures reward risk-taking with no personal downside for traders
Risk management teams are often underfunded and outranked by traders
Banks frequently ignore red flags when a trader is profitable

faq.question: Why don't bank controls prevent rogue trading?
faq.answer: Traders understand the control systems and know how to circumvent them. Risk management teams are often seen as cost centers and lack authority to challenge profitable trading desks. Revenue generation outranks risk management.

faq.question: Could technology prevent rogue trading?
faq.answer: AI-powered surveillance can detect unusual patterns faster than humans. But determined insiders with system knowledge can still find workarounds. Technology helps but cannot replace a culture where risk management has genuine authority.
